title: Open balls and open sets
objectives: Prove that open balls are open and that unions of open sets are open.

screens.title: Room to move
screens.prose: The point $y = (0.3, 0.4)$ sits inside the unit ball $B(0, 1)$. Pick a metric with the first control. Grow the small ball $B(y, s)$ until it just fits inside.
screens.question: For each metric, what is the largest $s$ with $B(y, s) \subseteq B(0, 1)$?

hints.text: Slide $s$ until the small ball touches the big one.
Each time the fit is $1 - d(0, y)$.

feedback.correct: Right. The room is always 1 minus the distance already used.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Grow the small ball in each metric until it touches.

byKey.d1-dist: 0.7 is how far $y$ is from 0 in $d_1$. The room left is $1 - 0.7$.

explain.text: The fits are 0.5 in $d_2$, 0.3 in $d_1$ and 0.6 in $d_\infty$. Each is $1 - d(0, y)$: the radius minus the distance already used.

screens.title: A radius that always works
screens.prose: A set $U$ is **open** when every point of $U$ has some ball $B(y, s)$, with $s > 0$, inside $U$. Take $y \in B(x, r)$ in any metric space, and write $d$ for $d(x, y)$.
screens.question: Give a radius $s$, in terms of $r$ and $d$, with $B(y, s) \subseteq B(x, r)$.

hints.text: The hook's answers were all $1 - d(0, y)$.
Replace 1 by $r$.

feedback.correct: Right. $s = r - d(x, y)$, positive because $d(x, y) < r$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The room left is the radius minus the distance used.

byKey.same: Radius $r$ round $y$ reaches past $x$'s ball on the far side.
byKey.dist: $d$ is the distance used up, not the room left.

explain.text: From $y$ we have used $d(x, y)$ of the radius $r$. So $s = r - d$ is the room left, and it is positive.

screens.title: Open balls are open
screens.prose: Now the proof, in any metric space. Two lines are tempting but flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $y \in B(x, r)$, so $d(x, y) < r$.
Put $s = r - d(x, y)$, which is positive.
Let $d(y, z) < s$. By the triangle inequality, $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.
So $d(x, z) < d(x, y) + s = r$. Hence $B(y, s) \subseteq B(x, r)$, and the ball is open. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: Take $y = (0.9, 0)$ in the unit disc. $B(y, 1)$ reaches $(1.8, 0)$, outside the disc.
Near the edge $d(x, y)$ is nearly $r$. At $y = (0.9, 0)$ the ball of radius 0.9 reaches $(1.8, 0)$.

hints.text: Choose the radius before testing a point $z$.
The radius is the one you just found.
Point, radius, triangle inequality, conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. The triangle inequality does the work.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Fix $y$, choose $s$, then test any $z$ within $s$ of $y$.

byKey.d1: You kept the same radius. Near the edge that ball sticks out.
byKey.d2: You used the distance from the centre. It is largest exactly where the room is smallest.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Choose $s = r - d(x, y)$. Any $z$ within $s$ of $y$ has $d(x, z) < d(x, y) + s = r$ by the triangle inequality. So every point of the ball has a ball inside it.

screens.title: Is that the biggest fit?
screens.prose: In the plane with $d_2$, take $y \in B(x, r)$ and $s = r - d(x, y)$. Could a larger radius $s' > s$ also fit?
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: No. Along the ray from $x$ through $y$, $B(y, s')$ holds points at distance $d(x, y) + t$ for $t < s'$, some above $r$.
Yes. The boundary is curved, so there is always a little extra room.
options.why: You looked away from the ray. Along the ray through $y$ the boundary is met at distance exactly $s$.

options.text: Yes, up to $2s$, by the triangle inequality.
options.why: The triangle inequality gives an upper bound on $d(x, z)$. It cannot grant extra room.

hints.text: Walk from $y$ straight away from $x$.
The ball first meets the circle at $w$.
$w$ is $s$ from $y$ and $r$ from $x$.

feedback.correct: Right. In a normed space $r - d(x, y)$ is the exact fit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the ray from $x$ through $y$.

explain.text: Along the ray, $d(x, z) = d(x, y) + d(y, z)$ exactly. So any radius past $s$ leaves the ball. In a general metric space the fit can be larger, as the discrete metric will show.

screens.title: A disc inside a diamond
screens.prose: Now mix metrics. Find the largest Euclidean ball $B_2(y, s)$ round $y = (0.3, 0.4)$ inside the taxicab ball $B_1(0, 1)$.
screens.question: What is the largest such $s$? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 0.2121: $\tfrac{0.3}{\sqrt2}$, the distance to the line $x + y = 1$.

hints.text: The nearest edge is $x + y = 1$.
The dashed segment meets that edge at a right angle.
Distance to $x + y = 1$ is $\tfrac{|0.3 + 0.4 - 1|}{\sqrt2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Measure the straight-line distance to the edge $x + y = 1$.

byKey.taxi: 0.3 is the taxicab room, $1 - d_1(0, y)$. A Euclidean ball is round, so it touches the edge sooner.
byKey.disc: 0.5 is the room inside the Euclidean disc. The diamond is smaller.

explain.text: The straight-line distance from $(0.3, 0.4)$ to $x + y = 1$ is $\tfrac{0.3}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.2121$. So every point of a $d_1$-open set has a $d_2$ ball inside, and the reverse holds too.

screens.title: Equivalent metrics, same open sets
screens.prose: Suppose $a\,d(x, y) \le d'(x, y) \le b\,d(x, y)$ for all $x, y$, with constants $a, b > 0$. We show a $d$-open set $U$ is $d'$-open.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x \in U$. Since $U$ is $d$-open, $B_d(x, r) \subseteq U$ for some $r > 0$.
If $d'(x, y) < ar$, then $d(x, y) \le \tfrac{d'(x, y)}{a} < r$, using $a\,d \le d'$.
So $B_{d'}(x, ar) \subseteq B_d(x, r) \subseteq U$, and $U$ is $d'$-open.
Likewise $d' \le b\,d$ gives $B_d(x, \tfrac{r}{b}) \subseteq B_{d'}(x, r)$, so $d'$-open sets are $d$-open. $\blacksquare$
So $B_{d'}(x, r) \subseteq B_d(x, r)$, since $d' \ge a\,d$.
lines.why: You dropped the constant. With $a < 1$, $d'(x, y) < r$ allows $d(x, y)$ up to $\tfrac{r}{a}$, past $r$.

hints.text: Shrink the radius by the factor $a$.
Ball in $U$, the inequality, the inclusion, then the other direction.

feedback.correct: Right. Each ball of one metric holds a ball of the other.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from the $d$-ball inside $U$.

byKey.d1: You kept radius $r$ in the new metric. The constant $a$ must shrink it.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: A $d'$-ball of radius $ar$ sits inside the $d$-ball of radius $r$. A $d$-ball of radius $\tfrac{r}{b}$ sits inside the $d'$-ball. With l1's $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$, all three metrics on the plane have the same open sets.

screens.title: Unions of open sets
screens.prose: Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be any family of open sets, possibly infinite. One line is tempting but flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof that $\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$ is open in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Then $x \in U_\beta$ for some one member $U_\beta$.
$U_\beta$ is open, so $B(x, r) \subseteq U_\beta$ for some $r > 0$.
And $U_\beta \subseteq \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$, so $B(x, r)$ lies in the union. $\blacksquare$
Take $r$ to be the smallest of the radii of all the members.
lines.why: Infinitely many radii may have no smallest positive one: $\tfrac1n$ shrinks to 0. One member is enough.

hints.text: A point of the union lies in at least one member.
That member's ball already lies in the union.

feedback.correct: Right. One member supplies the ball.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick one member that holds $x$.

byKey.d1: You tried to use every member at once. The smallest of infinitely many radii can be 0.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: A point of the union lies in one member $U_\beta$. Its ball inside $U_\beta$ is inside the union. No minimum over the family is needed, so any union works.

screens.title: Two open sets at once
screens.prose: Let $x \in U_1 \cap U_2$, both open, with $B(x, r_1) \subseteq U_1$ and $B(x, r_2) \subseteq U_2$.
screens.question: Give a radius $r$ with $B(x, r) \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$.

hints.text: The ball must fit inside both.
Take the smaller radius.

feedback.correct: Right. The smaller ball fits inside both.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which radius fits inside both sets?

byKey.max: The larger ball fits in one set but may stick out of the other.
byKey.sum: Adding radii gives a bigger ball, which fits in neither for sure.

explain.text: $B(x, \min(r_1, r_2))$ lies in both balls, so in both sets. For finitely many sets the minimum of finitely many positive radii is still positive.

screens.title: Infinitely many at once
screens.prose: Now intersect infinitely many: $\bigcap_{n \ge 1} B_2(0, 1 + \tfrac1n)$. Slide $n$ and watch the balls close in.
screens.question: Is the intersection open?

options.text: No. It is the closed disc, and $(1, 0)$ lies in it with no ball inside.
Yes. An intersection of open sets is open.
options.why: That holds for finitely many. Here the radii $1 + \tfrac1n$ shrink to 1, and no minimum is left.

options.text: It is the open unit disc, so yes.
options.why: $(1, 0)$ has $d_2 = 1 < 1 + \tfrac1n$ for every $n$, so it is in the intersection.

hints.text: Is $(1, 0)$ in every ball?
Every ball reaches past $(1, 0)$.
Any ball round $(1, 0)$ contains points at distance above 1.

feedback.correct: Right. Infinite intersections can close up.

explain.text: A point is in every ball exactly when $d_2 \le 1$, so the intersection is the closed unit disc. Round $(1, 0)$ every ball holds points with $d_2 > 1$. `analysis` l23 met the same thing on the line.

screens.title: Same radius, same fit?
screens.prose: A learner writes: "For $y \in B(x, r)$, the ball $B(y, r)$ has the same size. So it fits inside $B(x, r)$."
screens.question: Take the unit disc and $y = (0.9, 0)$. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: $B(y, 1)$ reaches $(1.8, 0)$, outside the disc. Same size does not mean inside.
Nothing: two balls of the same radius always nest.
options.why: You treated equal size as inclusion. The balls have different centres, so one can stick out of the other.

options.text: It works once $r$ is replaced by $\tfrac{r}{2}$.
options.why: At $y = (0.9, 0)$ the room left is $0.1$, far below $\tfrac12$. The radius must depend on $y$.

hints.text: Draw $B(y, 1)$ in your head.
$y$ is only 0.1 from the edge.

feedback.correct: Right. The fit must shrink near the edge.

byKey.fine: You assumed a ball of the same radius fits. Moved off-centre, it sticks out past the edge.

explain.text: $B((0.9, 0), 1)$ reaches $(1.8, 0)$. The radius that fits is $1 - 0.9 = 0.1$. It depends on how close $y$ is to the edge.

screens.title: The discrete metric
screens.prose: On any set $X$ the discrete metric is $d(x, y) = 1$ for $x \ne y$ and 0 for $x = y$. So $B(x, 1) = \{x\}$, while $B(x, 1.01) = X$.
screens.question: Which sets of $X$ are open in the discrete metric?

options.text: Every set: each point $x$ of a set $A$ has $B(x, 1) = \{x\} \subseteq A$.
Only $\varnothing$, the singletons and $X$, the balls themselves.
options.why: You listed the balls. Unions of open sets are open, and every set is a union of singletons.

options.text: Only $\varnothing$ and $X$, since balls jump from a point to everything.
options.why: The jump is in radius, not in sets. Radius 1 gives a singleton, which is open.

hints.text: Which ball round $x$ is as small as possible?
$B(x, 1)$ is a single point.
A singleton fits inside any set holding $x$.

explain.text: Every singleton is the ball $B(x, 1)$, so it is open. Any set is a union of singletons, hence open. Here the largest fit can exceed $r - d(x, y)$.

screens.title: Room inside a risk limit
screens.prose: Two desks hold exposures $x = (\text{£}0.3\text{m}, \text{£}0.4\text{m})$. Limit A caps each desk: $|x_k| < \text{£}1\text{m}$, an open $d_\infty$ ball. Limit B caps the total: $|x_1| + |x_2| < \text{£}1\text{m}$, an open $d_1$ ball.
screens.question: How far, in £m, can the exposures move in any direction and stay inside each limit? Use that limit's own metric.

hints.text: The room is the limit minus the distance already used.
$x$ has $d_\infty = 0.4$ and $d_1 = 0.7$.

feedback.correct: Right. £0.6m of room under limit A, £0.3m under limit B.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the exposure already used from £1m.

byKey.used: £0.4m is the larger exposure, already used. The room is what is left.
byKey.used1: £0.7m is the total already used. The room left is £0.3m.

explain.text: Limit A leaves $1 - 0.4 = 0.6$, so £0.6m in any direction, and limit B leaves $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$, so £0.3m of combined moves. Both limit sets are open, so a position strictly inside always has some room.

ideas: A set is open when each of its points has a ball $B(y, s)$, $s > 0$, inside it. For $y \in B(x, r)$ the radius $s = r - d(x, y)$ works, by the triangle inequality.
Any union of open sets is open, and so is a finite intersection, with radius $\min(r_1, r_2)$. An infinite intersection can fail: $\bigcap B_2(0, 1 + \tfrac1n)$ is the closed disc.
If $a\,d \le d' \le b\,d$ with $a, b > 0$, the two metrics have the same open sets; $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ do. In the discrete metric every set is open.

formula.name: The radius that fits
formula.tex: y \in B(x, r) \implies B\big(y, r - d(x, y)\big) \subseteq B(x, r)
formula.note: The triangle inequality gives $d(x, z) < d(x, y) + s = r$.

summary.trap: A ball round $y$ of the same radius $r$ need not fit inside $B(x, r)$. At $(0.9, 0)$ in the unit disc only 0.1 fits.

quiz.prose: In $d_\infty$ take the unit ball $B_\infty(0, 1)$, the open square, and the point $y = (0.2, 0.5)$.
quiz.question: What is the largest $s$ with $B_\infty(y, s) \subseteq B_\infty(0, 1)$?

feedback.correct: Right. The top edge is 0.5 away.

byKey.taxi: 0.3 is $1 - d_1(0, y)$. The square's room uses $d_\infty$.
byKey.small: 0.8 is the room to the side edge. The top edge is nearer.

explain.text: $d_\infty(0, y) = \max(0.2, 0.5) = 0.5$, so $s = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5$. The top edge $y_2 = 1$ is the nearest.

quiz.prose: Subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric.
quiz.question: Which sets are open? Select all that apply.

options.why: Every ball round 0 holds negative numbers, which are not in the set.

options.text: $(0, \infty)$

options.why: A single point holds no interval round itself in the usual metric.

options.text: $\mathbb{R}$

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for a point with no interval round it inside the set.

explain.text: $(0, 1)$, $(0, \infty)$ and $\mathbb{R}$ give each point an interval inside. $[0, 1)$ fails at 0 and $\{0\}$ fails at 0.

quiz.prose: Each $[\tfrac1n, 1 - \tfrac1n]$ for $n \ge 3$ is a closed interval.
quiz.question: What is $\bigcup_{n \ge 3} [\tfrac1n, 1 - \tfrac1n]$, and is it open?

options.text: $(0, 1)$, which is open
$[0, 1]$, which is closed
options.why: 0 lies in no member, since $\tfrac1n > 0$ for every $n$.

options.text: A closed set, since a union of closed sets is closed
options.why: That holds for finitely many. Infinitely many closed sets can union to an open set.

feedback.correct: Right. Every point of $(0, 1)$ is caught by some member.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which points of $[0, 1]$ lie in some member?

explain.text: Each $x \in (0, 1)$ lies in $[\tfrac1n, 1 - \tfrac1n]$ once $n$ is large, while 0 and 1 never do. So the union is $(0, 1)$, which is open.

quiz.prose: A point $y$ lies in $B(x_1, r_1) \cap B(x_2, r_2)$, with $d_1 = d(x_1, y)$ and $d_2 = d(x_2, y)$.
quiz.question: Which radius $s$ is sure to give $B(y, s)$ inside the intersection?

options.why: You kept the radii of the big balls. Room round $y$ must subtract the distance already used.
The larger room fits one ball but may stick out of the other.

feedback.correct: Right. Room in each ball, then the smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the room inside each ball first.

explain.text: $B(y, r_k - d_k)$ fits inside $B(x_k, r_k)$ for each $k$. The smaller of the two radii fits inside both.
